title_original: Colin Meloy on the Magic of Wildwood and 25 Years of The Decemberists
excerpt_original: Even before The Decemberists were formed in 2000, Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis were working on ideas for their epic, Portland-set fantasy novel Wildwood, which was finally completed and released in 2011, spanning more than 500 pages. Before the book hit shelves, LAIKA optioned…

blocks.text: Even before The Decemberists were formed in 2000, Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis were working on ideas for their epic, Portland-set fantasy novel Wildwood , which was finally completed and released in 2011, spanning more than 500 pages. Before the book hit shelves, LAIKA optioned the rights to adapt the tale into a stop-motion feature. But Travis Knight’s company, in its nascent stages only a few years after their debut Coraline , wasn’t quite ready to make the leap into a story of this scale and ambition.

The extensive production wouldn’t begin until around a decade later and, after that intricate, handmade process, Wildwood at last premiered this fall. The result is a staggering accomplishment that’s also set a record for the longest stop-motion feature animation of all time, and which uses every second of screentime to transport viewers into a magical world full of characters and details that could sprout a thousand other stories.

As the film crosses its first month of release, with word of mouth steadily growing, I had the pleasure of speaking to Meloy—who also brought the Decemberists back together to record the new track “The Better Part of Bravery”—about seeing LAIKA’s creation come to life, the adaptation process, taking on serious issues in animation, how indie music has changed in the 25 years since his band’s debut album, and much more.

The Film Stage: I know you teamed with LAIKA in 2011 for the teaser for your book and they optioned it before Wildwood was even finished. Then it was another decade before production began. Were you having any conversations about the film in that time?

links.text: for the teaser for your book

blocks.text: Colin Meloy: I was just waiting. I mean, there were conversations. They were kind of considering directors. They were working on drafts of the screenplay. We were seeing concept art. Every year or two, we’d go up there and see what they were working on, and they would show us some little teaser of something, to show that there was progress being made. And always, I feel like at the end of it, Travis [Knight] would assure me that they were making the film eventually, that they just had to develop new technologies in stop motion to be able to do it. He was very clear about that. And also, he felt like they needed to get more films under their belt before they could take it on. To be honest, I thought that maybe he was going to blow smoke up my ass. But he made good on his word. I think they really did need to—I mean, you can see it on the screen. It is like kind of an incredible achievement.
Yeah, I love how Caleb Deschanel actually came on as a cinematographer, which is quite rare for an animated film to have such a level of craft. Did you ever talk to him about his process?

We met Caleb while he was working. And yeah, I thought it was extraordinary. You know, you think back to some of those films that he’s worked on—it’s sort of like jaw-dropping. I think The Black Stallion is one of the first films I remember going to see in the cinema with my dad. Even to this day, you think about the cinematography, and that is just phenomenal. And not to mention his involvement with Twin Peaks and directing in Twin Peaks . So yeah: we were a little starstruck meeting him.

One thing I was delighted by was how the film doesn’t feel neutered at all to appeal to the widest possible audience. With the robot heart being ripped out, a decapitation, and more, it really feels like one of those films that marks a transition from childhood to adulthood for viewing experiences. Were you delighted to see LAIKA push certain boundaries in this way? Did you have similar touchstones growing up?

Oh, absolutely. Yeah. Those films that ended up being the kind of touchstones that I hear a lot of people talking about when they’re talking about Wildwood —like putting it into the same place as The Dark Crystal and The Secret of NIMH and Watership Down . People being traumatized! But, you know, those are the films that stick with you. Those are the kids’ movies— The NeverEnding Story —these things where it’s like: the stakes are real and you get a little frightened. But they’re well-made and they’re well-considered stories, so you don’t feel like you’re being pandered to or taken advantage of as a viewer.

I think, even as kids, you understand that. You can handle that because it feels like you’re being taken seriously. I think of Watership Down as dealing with these very serious issues about how a community works and how a community comes together to fight against, like, a fascist oppressor. And told by rabbits—talking rabbits! And I think it’s important for kids to learn that stuff and see it early on, even if it might be frightening, and exposing them to an adult world that is very real and stuff that you may come up against in your life. So I’m thrilled that Wildwood is working in that tradition.
I’ve never seen an animated film quite so lovingly detail a real-life place as this one does with Portland. I wanted to take my family to go visit it right away.
Yeah, you should come.
It’s captured in this pre-tech boom, peak-indie era as a quaint, lovely place. From your perspective, does watching the film feel like a time capsule at all, or is it kind of how it is?

A little bit because, I mean, it’s funny: people talking about it being a love letter to Portland at a time when Portland kind of needs a little bit of a shot in the arm. When I was writing the novel, it was peak Portland then, when the New York Times was writing a thing about Portland every week. There were bands coming out and getting known. Portlandia was happening. At that point it felt like Portland didn’t need a love letter. If anything, everybody was like, “Can you just leave us alone a little bit?”

But now it’s interesting—like 15, 16 years later—I think particularly in that opening sequence where you see Voodoo Doughnuts and you see the Unipiper and all the kind weird Portland stuff, which I think in maybe in 2011, 2010 I would have maybe rolled my eyes at a little bit. But seeing it now, it’s kind of like, “Yes, yes, that’s my city, that’s my weird town. I love it.”

As a long-time fan of the Decemberists, I’d say all your albums are very cinematic, but I think of The Hazards of Love or The Crane Wife would make for incredible films in their own right. Have you ever fantasized about adapting them? Or just as you were writing all the lyrics, thinking, who would be the perfect director to adapt this?

You know, I haven’t really. I mean, there has been talk along the way about the sort of jukebox musical about Decemberists stuff. And people have staged The Hazards of Love —high schools and community theaters across the country have done that. Bless their souls. But it’s not something that I’ve ever been super interested in, because I just feel like a band performing those songs on an album is really the medium that they were intended for, in my mind.

links.text: have staged The Hazards of Love

blocks.text: Next year is 25 years since the debut album Castaways and Cutouts . What are your reflections on that milestone and how do you think indie music has evolved since that special moment?

Yeah, I am starting to think about it. We are kind of trying to think about how we can mark that occasion and trying to find the old, old tapes and see if there’s anything out there hidden. Yeah, I think things have changed a lot, but there’s still so much good indie music being made—maybe even more so. I think the major-label system being what it is. There’s just so many more opportunities for musicians to get their music out there than there ever was then, when the idea of peer-to-peer file sharing was kind of in its nascence. So yeah: it’s changed and not changed.
Back to Wildwood , for “The Better Part of Bravery,” when you were writing it, did you know it would be used as an end-credits song and what kind of animation it would be paired with?

Oh, I just wrote the song. I had no idea. I mean, particularly the last six months, seven months before the opening of Wildwood , it’s just everybody working and hoping that it all comes together. It felt like a community theater putting on a production. It’s like, “I built the set. Here it is. Great.” I wrote the song and turned it in and knew that it was being used, and was like, “I guess it’s good.” I mean, there was so much going on those last seven months, and it was just sort of a hope and a prayer that it would come together, it would cut together well. But we’ve been working on this thing for long enough, and Travis and I have been in contact enough and discussing the screenplay and the production—I mean, all that—that everybody was on the same page. So whatever you did, it was going to slot in. And I think that’s exactly sort of what happened.

Dario Marianelli’s score is amazing. I’m curious, you’re an artist and a musician in your own right. What is it like to see a composer give a deeper musical life to the film? Did you first hear the score in concert with the film, or was it separate?

Yeah, I didn’t hear it until the finished thing, until I saw it on the screen. I wasn’t really much in contact with Dario, even though I’d written these songs that he was then [scoring], which I was able to just record as my demos at home and then pass on. And then he had to bring them to the actors and record them and modulate them as needed. So he had the real challenge there. I had the easy job of just writing the thing and demoing it. But I thought he did a fantastic job. And just the way that he approached it, the musicality feels very unconventional throughout a lot of it. It feels very handmade, using these sort of old Renaissance instruments, folk instruments, a lot of acoustic instruments. He had a nyckelharpa person come into his studio and play. I just think that he definitely got the idea that this should be kind of a handmade piece of music as he’s scoring it. And I think he succeeded.

The movie has been out for a month now, and there was so much talk about the budget and the box office around the time of release. And then it’s great to see, these past few weeks, people really are turning out and the word of mouth has been great. Being behind the longest stop-motion animation ever and these huge milestones, what have the last few weeks been like compared to the opening-week press?

It has been extraordinary. I mean, just having no idea how it would be received, because I feel like I was so close to it, and I remember seeing an early cut of it in April when I was working on the end-credit song. And having watched it in my studio, I remember coming in, and Carson Ellis—who’s the illustrator, my wife—was waiting to see it in the theater. So she asked, “How was it?” And I just didn’t know. I was like, “I think it’s good. I don’t know.” It was just one of those things, you’re just like, “I have no idea. It could go both ways.” I mean, it was clearly a beautiful piece of work. But being so close to the story and the characters, I just couldn’t say. So of course it was this massive relief when it premiered in London and all of a sudden it was just, like, every review across the board was just, like, five stars, and it was, like, 100% or whatever on the Tomato-ma-meter, which I just wasn’t even really aware was a thing—really—until this moment. So that was just really exciting.

With your novel being 500-plus pages, I wanted to ask about Chris Butler’s adaptation process. The world of Wildwood is so rich in detail that I almost wanted to live in it even longer and learn more about all the characters, but there has to be painful cuts in an adaptation process. How much in touch was he with you about that while he was writing, or was it more like you saw the script after he did his job?

I saw two drafts of the screenplay and gave notes on it. But I never—from the outset, and I was clear about this—I didn’t want to be [involved]. At the beginning, Travis was basically like, “You can be as involved in this as you want to or not want to.” And I think in collaborations like this where I don’t see myself as a filmmaker or a screenwriter, I felt perfectly comfortable just being like, “You guys go cook, you know, I’m good.” And I saw the screenplay. I was surprised how much of it was intact, actually. I was prepared for there to be not only huge cuts, but also major diversions in plot and things like that, which I’ve seen happen with other adaptations of books. So I was surprised—I was kind of flattered. It was like, “Oh, I guess the story is okay if they want to keep it as it is.”

It was my first novel, so there’s a little bit of first-novel jitters in there. I mean, inevitably there’s backstory stuff that you lose, with the lore of the coyotes and the South Wood government—it’s basically a kind of a fascist, authoritarian governance coming into play, which is a lot, then kind of builds up to that end moment. You kind of had to move focus away from that and more towards the Alexandra story. And that’s fine. I think they made smart decisions in that sense.
You had mentioned that, in the early 2000s, you even wrote an 80-page draft that was even darker.

Well, there was a ton of stuff from that that we used. I mean, that story—which you can read, I serialized it on my Substack , the 80 pages that I did write. But it did all hinge around this mechanical boy prince who has been… this cog has been lost, is broken, and it has to be rebuilt. The stuff that happens in Under Wildwood , like the Unadoptables at the orphanage with Curtis’ sisters, that all is taken from that original story as well. So we kind of took the best bits and tried to move it into Wildwood .
Lastly, have you been surprised at any part of the reaction to the film?

The crow-defender community has really taken umbrage with the fact that the crows are maligned. And I didn’t really mean to malign crows. It’s really based on Irish mythology—these spirits called sluagh that often took the shape of birds and would steal babies from their cribs. And I just went with crows, and it really brought out the pro-crow community.
You never know what’s going to happen.
You’re going to offend somebody. My apologies.
Wildwood is now in theaters.
